abstract: The spinal cord contains cell types critical for motor, sensory, and autonomic function, many of which are implicated in neurological disease and injury. Yet no shared molecular framework links human spinal cord cell types to the animal models used to study them. Here, we present a cross-species atlas integrating single-nucleus gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and spatial transcriptomics from over one million nuclei spanning cervical to sacral segments in human, macaque, and mouse. Consensus clustering resolves 111 cell type groups replicable across all three species, whose spatial distributions map spinal laminae and nuclei, including Clarke's column. Identity and laminar organization are highly conserved, yet abundance and expression are allometrically scaled, with the dorsal horn being the principal site of divergence, concentrated in neurotransmitter receptor genes and including a primate-specific glycine receptor subunit switch. Sequence models uncover a conserved transcription factor grammar and nominate motifs underlying enhancer-adeno-associated virus (AAV) access to a divergent dorsal horn population.
hook: A spinal cord atlas of over a million nuclei finds 111 cell type groups shared by human, macaque and mouse.

readout.label: Cell type groups shared across three species

summary: Researchers combined single-nucleus gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and spatial data from over one million nuclei across three species. Cell identity and layout are highly conserved, while the dorsal horn differs most, including a primate-specific glycine receptor subunit switch. The atlas is descriptive, and the enhancer predictions for targeting cells with viral vectors still need testing.
title: A consensus spinal cord cell-type atlas across mouse, macaque, and human.
